Good summary of the state of the Left

This is a very descriptive piece about the predicament of today's left as the working class abandons it.

The centre of gravity of the left today is the university lecturer. Around that you have students, schoolteachers, civil servants, other professionals, in concentric circles of distance. The working poor are nowhere near that centre of gravity, and while they are not yet lost as left voters, they are steadily moving in that direction.

(As an aside, that is a point of confusion in much recent psephology. The recent gains by the right, in various elections, have come overwhelmingly from the working class. That does not represent overwhelming support for the right by the working class, merely that the old dominance of the left of that bloc has dwindled)

As I say, the poor, to a degree, still vote left, but the left has lost contact with their concerns. That is the point of this Guardian piece, and also of Chris Arnade's observational tweetstorms. The left is concerned with justice and diversity, the poor with jobs.

Harris in The Guardian puts much wait on the "precariat"--working people without steady full-time jobs. How would a left that actually diverted attention from Social Justice to that issue address these people's problems?

Let me talk about pubs.

In Britain in the 1980s, a lot of people were upset about pubs. Mostly, pubs were either run by breweries, or owned by breweries and leased by them to tenants who ran them. The deal was that they would only sell beer made by the one brewery. It was widely complained that this system reduced customer choice and that customers were getting a bad deal.

In 1989, the government took action, and orders were made under monopolies laws to break up the tied pub: breweries were limited in the number of pubs they could own, and pubs were to be allowed to carry "guest beers" from other breweries.

25 years later, about half of the pubs are gone. When the market got a bit tougher, there wasn't enough profit in the business to enable the owners to keep going.

A case could be made for saying something similar has happened to jobs. The long struggle of the left through the twentieth century was to improve the position of employees, just as the Beer Orders were to improve the position of pub customers. Now there is no appetite in the market for being an employer in the way that 20th century companies were.

Yes, technical shifts have been the trigger of the problem, but that can be over-emphasised. After all, industry has not so far ceased to need low-skilled workers: the Guardian piece discusses the casual, part-time and self-employed work that is being done today by the children of those who had long-term steady employment.

If the workers would prefer those steady jobs to their membership of the "precariat", then maybe a century of legislative activity to make giving people steady jobs less profitable was a mistake. A modern left that actually cared more about the working class than about race, gender and microaggressions, might come up with models under which companies could profitably employ people long-term on reliable wages. Like the traditional pub, that might mean vertical integration: companies playing a bigger part in their employees' lives, rather than being forced to enable them to go elsewhere. Also like the old pub, it would mean some restrictions on the freedom of the employee to look for a better deal at the drop of a hat. If stability and security are what today's workers are lacking, the law should not be denying them.

Is that a bad deal? I don't know. What I can see is that nobody on the left even thinks these problems are serious enough to actually work on. Technology and globalisation have caused the problems, and to try to solve them is racist and backwards. I am not convinced.
